functionalObligations.text: a bettor's position is a transferable NFT carrying a payout struck against the pool; no operation splits pool collateral into complementary outcome claims and none recombines them
functionalObligations.note: residue, and the third answer this category gives to the first structural claim. Polymarket implements a state partition (polymarket.json F1), Kalshi implements a price identity (kalshi.json F3), and Azuro implements neither: the contingent claim is one-sided and unitary, the pool holds the other side implicitly, and there is no object to split or merge. `Py` splits along time and does not apply; nothing in the 58 names a one-sided tokenised contingent claim on a pool either.

functionalObligations.text: a single protocol-wide liquidity pool is the counterparty to every bet, writing a non-linear event-contingent payoff, so no bettor ever faces another bettor
functionalObligations.note: residue, confirming the corpus. `Pl` is lending; `Cv` requires adjudicated claims against pooled premium; `Op` requires a strike and an expiry. Note the relation to the category's second structural claim: this is the third clearing form in five applications — a pool that is principal to every trade with no novation and no substitution — and the vocabulary names none of the three.

functionalObligations.text: the price of an outcome is the normalised inverse of the pool's virtual fund for that outcome, loaded with a spread allocated inversely to the outcome's probability under a total-margin constraint, and every bet moves the virtual funds so the odds worsen against incoming flow
functionalObligations.note: residue, confirming the corpus. The closed form is published: o_i = sum(F)/F_i, p_i = 1/o_i, s_i = 1 - p_i*o_i with s_i/s_j = p_j/p_i, and the update F_i <- F_i - a with the other funds scaled by their share. None of `Cp`, `Wg`, `St`, `Cl` or `Pm` describes it, because all five price an ASSET against another asset or against an external reference and this prices a STATE against the pool's own exposure. The virtual funds are pricing parameters deliberately decoupled from the pool's real balance, so the curve is not even a function of the inventory it claims to represent.

functionalObligations.text: the odds struck at the moment of the bet are locked for that bettor and fix the payout, while the curve continues to move for everyone after
functionalObligations.note: residue. payout = o_i * (1 - s_i) * a, fixed at bet time. There is no symbol for a quoted-and-locked payoff drawn from a continuously repriced pool; `Rf` (request for quote) names a signed maker quote in a bilateral trade, not a quote struck against a pool's own moving curve, and `Op` requires a strike and an expiry rather than a struck price.

functionalObligations.text: each Condition reserves a fixed Reinforcement of pool liquidity at creation, immutable thereafter, which both seeds the outcome pricing and bounds the pool's worst-case loss on that Condition so simultaneous events cannot oversubscribe the same capital
functionalObligations.note: approximate; the corpus marker is right that this is the closest good fit in the whole vocabulary, and stage 1 sharpens why it is still not exact: `Rl` reserves a RESOURCE against a fulfilment, whereas Reinforcement reserves a WORST-CASE LOSS computed across an entire outcome vector, and it doubles as the price prior. It is a risk budget and a pricing seed in one object, and `Rl` carries neither role. Azuro's own marketing calls this 'concentrated liquidity', which would have made `Cl` an attractive and completely wrong choice: naming collision, not mechanism match.

functionalObligations.text: bets enter through a relayer that is the execution entry point for the whole protocol, taking the bettor's signed order and drawing sponsored fees and freebet amounts from a paymaster
functionalObligations.note: departure from the corpus, which records neither element; both are V3 components absent from the V2 public repository. `Gs` (sponsored-fee liability, paymaster) is an exact fit, down to the contract's name. `Au` is approximate: the relayer executes authority the bettor delegated by signing, which is the shape `Au` describes, but the scope is protocol-defined rather than user-configured. This pairing also warrants `Rl` (F5) under the tables and satisfies L20 and L21, which the corpus's Azuro element set could not.

functionalObligations.text: each liquidity deposit is a separate leaf of a segment tree over a 2K+1 array, a Condition's profit and loss is distributed across a leaf range, and the updates are lazy — annotated at parent nodes and pushed down only when a provider withdraws
functionalObligations.note: residue, and a departure from the corpus, which recorded `Sh` (stage-1 delta 4). A provider's claim is not a pro-rata share of one pot: it is a leaf with an entry position, and its value depends on WHICH Conditions resolved during its residence. That is neither `Sh` (proportional claim on a pool), nor `Ix` (a single global index), nor `Rb` (nominal rescaling). The LiquidityTree is a third accounting form the vocabulary does not have. The token standard of the provider's position is UNKNOWN — the docs do not say whether it is fungible, an NFT, or a bare accounting entry.

functionalObligations.text: a liquidity provider is locked for seven days from deposit and may withdraw at will thereafter
functionalObligations.note: residue. `Wq` is a queue of claimants waiting for liquidity that has not arrived; this is a per-deposit minimum holding period with no queue and no rationing. `Ep` gates transitions at shared epoch boundaries and this lock is dated from each deposit individually. Azuro's own documentation warns that positions held under a week will most likely be in the red, so the lock is economically load-bearing rather than administrative.

functionalObligations.text: one permissioned party creates and cancels events, seeds and reprices the sell-side odds, sets the reinforcement and margin, and then declares which outcome won
functionalObligations.note: residue, and a departure from the corpus, which recorded `Ex` AND `Sv` for this role; stage 1 finds both wrong. `Ex` misrepresents a single trusted party as an oracle — there is no feed, no aggregation and no medianizer; `Sv` is written for servicing a loan and does not reach 'sets the price and also decides who won'; `Oa` needs an assertion, a bond and a dispute window and there is none. Azuro's docs say Data Providers resolve 'in good faith' citing a bookmaker's published settlement rules, with AzuroDAO 'acting as the arbiter of last resort in case of disputes' — so the corpus's flat claim of 'no dispute path' is wrong as documented (stage-1 delta 1), but the arbitration MECHANISM is not specified on-chain anywhere stage 1 could find and is marked UNKNOWN. Dropping `Ex` and `Sv` leaves this application with no expressible resolution mechanism at all, which is the category's finding, not a gap in the spec.

functionalObligations.text: a Data Provider must post collateral up to the total Reinforcement it expects to use across all its active markets
functionalObligations.note: residue, and a stage-1 finding the corpus records no bond for at all (stage-1 delta 2). `Bs` is the nearest shape and does not fit: nothing in the documentation describes a slashing condition, so this is a bond against MISPRICING — capital sized to the exposure the party is allowed to create — rather than slashable first-loss capital against insolvency or against a false report.

functionalObligations.text: a Condition may be paused, and cancelling it refunds every bettor's stake instead of paying out
functionalObligations.note: `Gp` fits the pause. `Rd` is approximate for the refund: it names an unconditional right to draw a fixed amount back, but the act here unwinds an already-struck contingent claim at par, and no element names the annulment of a live claim as distinct from its settlement.

functionalObligations.text: a winning bettor claims the payout struck at bet time after the Condition is resolved
functionalObligations.note: good fit for the claim itself; the amount claimed is fixed by F4, which is residue.

functionalObligations.text: the pool quotes a price to buy back an open bet before the event concludes, extinguishing a live contingent claim early
functionalObligations.note: residue, and absent from the corpus record entirely — Cashout is a V3 feature (stage-1 delta 5). It is not `Rd` (there is no resolved payout to redeem against), not `Ob` (there is no counterparty), and not `Op` (there is no strike). A pool that will repurchase its own written liability at a quoted price before the state is known is a distinct mechanism with no symbol.

functionalObligations.text: a combination bet multiplies the odds of several legs into one payout while the pool's exposure to the combination is not the product of its exposures to the legs
functionalObligations.note: residue, confirming the corpus. A whole risk-management object — correlated exposure across simultaneously-priced conditions underwritten by one pool — with no representation in the vocabulary.

functionalObligations.text: pool revenue is divided among four named claimants: liquidity providers take 20% and the Data Provider 10% of the pool's profit or loss on each completed Condition, apps take a share, and AzuroDAO takes the residual computed by deducting all other rewards from monthly pool revenue
functionalObligations.note: `Fd` (candidate register) fits the distribution with a named residual claimant. Departure from the corpus on a neighbouring point: the corpus records `Em` (protocol-funded emissions) and stage 1 could not confirm at a primary source that protocol-funded emissions are currently paid (stage-1 delta 3). What is verifiable is a share of pool profit and loss and of spread revenue, which is `Fd`, not `Em`; a `RewardPool` repository exists but its live use is UNKNOWN. `Em` is therefore dropped from the construction. The split itself is mutable at AzuroDAO's discretion.

functionalObligations.text: an app's share is the LESSER of 70% of the revenue it generated and a monthly cap of 50% of the spread times the bet size summed over its bets
functionalObligations.note: residue. `Fd` (F15) names the fact of distribution but not a share capped by a DIFFERENT quantity from the one it is a share of, and there is no symbol for a frontend as a first-class revenue claimant of the protocol it fronts.

functionalObligations.text: when the pool loses, the liquidity providers', Data Provider's and DAO's rewards go negative, while an app's share can only ever be positive or zero
functionalObligations.note: residue. This is a declared order of loss-bearing across claimant classes, published in a fee schedule rather than encoded as a structure. `Tr` names declared seniority over a loss event and is the nearest, but there are no tranches, no principal and no waterfall — only a sign rule on a reward rate; `Sl` assigns a realised deficit to a claim class and there is no deficit here, just a negative share of a period's result. Neither is honest, so neither is used.

functionalObligations.text: protocol roles are tokenised by an Access contract and granted by the pool owner, so only permissioned parties may create Conditions, reprice odds or resolve them
functionalObligations.note: approximate, and a departure from the corpus, which records no access element for Azuro. `Aw` is a permission/identity gate and the function matches — a party without the role token cannot act — but `Aw` is written for gating holders of a claim, and here what is gated is an office, with the role itself being transferable as a token.

functionalObligations.text: pools are deployed by a factory behind beacon proxies, and the pool owner may attach new betting engines to a live pool
functionalObligations.note: good fit for the beacon-proxy upgradeability. Note two facts stage 1 established that bear on any check of this construction: no timelock is documented, so L15 (Up implies Tg or a bounded emergency process) is unsatisfied; and the deployed system is V3 while the only public contract repository covers V2 and has not been touched since 2025-01-29, so the source for the live system is UNKNOWN and every element above is grounded in documentation rather than in code (stage-1 delta 6).

paper.title: Azuro
paper.label: cat:prd:azuro
paper.blurb: A bettor stakes collateral on an outcome at odds quoted and locked at the moment of the bet, and holds the position as a transferable token. There is no counterparty on the other side: a single protocol-wide pool underwrites every bet, and the odds move against incoming flow because each bet shifts the virtual funds from which they are computed. The payout is fixed at bet time and claimed once the event resolves; a cancelled event refunds the stake instead, and the pool will also quote a price to buy an open bet back before the event concludes. The party that priced the event also resolves it --- a permissioned data provider creates the event, seeds and reprices the odds, sets the risk budget, and then declares which outcome won, resolving in good faith against a bookmaker's published settlement rules. The protocol's documentation names its DAO as arbiter of last resort in a dispute and specifies no mechanism for that arbitration anywhere on-chain, so the dispute path exists on paper and nowhere else.
paper.witnessReason: The element-set decomposition carries $Rl$ with no $Au$, which makes this the only protocol in the corpus rejected on a \emph{warrant} --- an element present that nothing consumes --- rather than on a requirement alone. The witness repairs that with $Au$ and $Gs$ on evidence: the live protocol routes every bet through a relayer that executes the bettor's signed order and draws sponsored fees from a paymaster, both documented in the architecture and both absent from the public contract repository, which covers a superseded version. $Ex$ and $Sv$ are dropped because there is no feed, no aggregation and no medianizer, and because servicing discretion is written for a loan rather than for a party that sets the price and then decides who won; $Sh$ is dropped because a provider's claim is a leaf of a segment tree whose value depends on which events resolved during its residence; $Em$ is dropped because what is documented is a share of the pool's profit and loss, which is $Fd$. Dropping the truth elements leaves this venue with no expressible resolution mechanism at all, and that is the finding rather than a defect in the witness.
paper.residueNote: What the witness cannot say is almost everything that makes this a betting protocol rather than an exchange. A pool that is principal to every trade, writing a non-linear event-contingent payoff, has no element; nor has a curve that prices a \emph{state} against the pool's own exposure rather than an asset against an asset; nor has a payoff quoted and locked for one bettor while that curve keeps moving for the next. The resource lock the witness does carry is the closest good fit in the whole vocabulary and is still not exact, because what is reserved is a worst-case loss across an entire outcome vector and it doubles as the pricing seed. The accounting is residue too: a provider's claim is a leaf with an entry position rather than a proportional share of a pot, and the vocabulary has no accounting form for it. What remains is the commercial arrangement --- early buy-back of a live claim, correlated exposure across combined legs, a frontend as a first-class revenue claimant, and an order of loss-bearing declared in a fee schedule rather than encoded as a structure.
